tasks.short: Prepare neighbourhood figures, meet civic, school and community groups about policing, plan community events with partners and write follow-up actions.

steps.what: Police sergeant prepares neighbourhood figures for the meeting
Police sergeant meets with civic, educational and community groups to discuss law enforcement subjects
Police sergeant plans community programs and events with partners by e-mail
Police sergeant writes follow-up actions after the meeting

tasks.design: An area dashboard ({BI}) shows anonymised incident counts per neighbourhood, so figures need no compiling. A shared planning page with partners ({DOCS}) holds event plans and follow-up actions with owners. Meeting groups and planning with partners stay with the sergeant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Figures were compiled by hand and plans agreed in long e-mail threads.
tasks.enabler_now: Police data can feed anonymised area dashboards, and shared pages hold joint plans.
tasks.still_hard: Trust in a neighbourhood is built in conversations, not dashboards.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing what residents are afraid to report.

reach.learn: Whether shared plans keep partners engaged.

evidence.claim: Police incident data can feed dashboards with anonymised counts per area.
Police data may only be shared outside the police in aggregated form unless the law allows otherwise.

assumptions: Boundary: from incident records to the action list; running events is outside.
Input contract: incidents recorded by officers; partners use the shared page; fallback is spreadsheets and e-mail.
Meeting and planning do not change.
Partners' time is outside the sergeant's savings.
research_questions: Are follow-up actions completed more often?

incremental.description: Police sergeant checks the area dashboard before meetings.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Most of this task is meeting people.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check the legal basis and time limits of detention, decide on release or transfer with the prosecutor, arrange transport, hand over property and paperwork, and record the release or transfer.

steps.what: Police sergeant checks the legal basis and time limits of each detention
Police sergeant directs release or transfer of prisoners after consulting the prosecutor
Police sergeant phones to arrange transport for the transfer
Police sergeant hands over property and paperwork to the prisoner or escort
Police sergeant writes the release or transfer in the custody log

tasks.design: The custody system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows each detainee's legal basis and the time limits that apply, with alerts before they run out. Transport is requested through the transport service's portal ({PARTNER_PORTAL}) from the detainee record, and the custody log fills from the actions recorded there. Deciding on release or transfer with the prosecutor and the handover stay with the sergeant; no decision is automated.
tasks.previous_blocker: Time limits were tracked on boards and transport arranged by phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Custody systems track time limits and link to transport requests.
tasks.still_hard: Urgent transfers and medical needs still need phone calls.
tasks.human_edge: Releasing a vulnerable person with a safe place to go.

evidence.claim: Custody systems can track legal time limits and raise alerts before they expire.
No adverse decision may rest solely on automated processing of police data without prior human intervention.

assumptions: Boundary: from custody records to the custody log; the court process is outside.
Input contract: detention data entered by custody officers; time limits set in law; fallback is the board and phone.
Deciding and handing over do not change.
Prosecutors' time is outside the sergeant's savings.

incremental.description: Police sergeant corrects detention data when alerts are wrong.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Decisions and handovers stay in person.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check equipment stock, requisition supplies, issue equipment to officers and record who holds what, chase items not returned and report damage.

steps.what: Police sergeant checks stock of equipment and supplies in the store
Police sergeant requisitions equipment and supplies from logistics by e-mail
Police sergeant issues equipment to officers and writes who has what
Police sergeant chases equipment not returned
Police sergeant reports damaged equipment

tasks.design: An equipment register ({OPS_SYSTEM}) records issue and return by scanning the item and the officer's pass, shows stock against minimum levels and lists overdue items. Requisitions go to logistics through the procurement portal ({PROCUREMENT}) from the stock view, and damage is reported in a short form. Deciding what to order and handing out equipment stay with the sergeant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stock was counted by hand, requisitions e-mailed and issues written in a book.
tasks.enabler_now: Equipment registers with barcode scanning and procurement portals exist.
tasks.still_hard: Items without barcodes still need counting.
tasks.human_edge: Making sure a new officer gets gear that actually fits.

evidence.claim: Equipment registers record issue and return by barcode scan and list overdue items.
Registers that link equipment to named officers can observe behaviour, so the works council must consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the store to damage reports; buying by logistics is outside.
Input contract: minimum levels set by the team chief; item barcodes applied by logistics; fallback is the book.
Deciding and issuing do not change.
Logistics' time is outside the sergeant's savings.

already_counted.description: Police sergeant reviews the stock view.

incremental.description: Police sergeant replaces worn barcode labels.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Items without barcodes still need counting.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Gather incidents, complaints and law changes that call for a policy change, draft the revised procedure, discuss it with the team, get the team chief's approval, publish it and explain it in briefings.

steps.what: Police sergeant gathers incidents, complaints and law changes that call for a policy change
Police sergeant develops and revises departmental policies and procedures

loop.input: The current procedure, the change reasons and the relevant law and instructions; no case data.
loop.output: A revised procedure with tracked changes, each rule citing its source.
loop.check: Code rejects rules without a cited source and shows changes against the current version; the sergeant edits and the team chief approves.
loop.stop: Approved by the team chief, or after two redrafts the sergeant writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Rewording procedures for new situations needs free text.

steps.what: Police sergeant discusses the draft with the team
Team chief approves the revised procedure
Police sergeant e-mails the procedure to all staff
Police sergeant implements the procedure by explaining it in briefings

tasks.design: A view on incident and complaint records ({BI}) shows patterns that call for a change. A bounded step drafts the revised procedure with tracked changes and a cited source per rule, and the sergeant edits it. After the team discussion and the team chief's approval, the document space ({DOCS}) publishes the new version to all staff. Explaining it in briefings stays with the sergeant; rules on working time also go to the works council.
tasks.previous_blocker: Procedures were rewritten by hand in text files and sent around by mail.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models draft revisions with sources; document spaces keep versions.
tasks.still_hard: Procedures must work on the street, not only on paper.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing which rule officers will quietly ignore and why.
tasks.altitude: The sergeant edits a drafted revision instead of rewriting it.

reach.learn: Whether tracked changes speed up approval.

evidence.claim: Language models can draft revisions of procedures with tracked changes and cited sources.
Rules on working and rest times need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from change reasons to the procedure explained; national policy is outside.
Input contract: law and instructions from police headquarters; incidents recorded by officers; fallback is writing by hand.
Discussing, approving and explaining do not change.
The team chief's time is outside the sergeant's savings.
research_questions: How much of the drafted revision is kept?

already_counted.description: Police sergeant reviews the patterns view.
Police sergeant edits the drafted revision.

incremental.description: Police sergeant keeps source texts current in the document space.

approvals.approved_version: The procedure as approved by the team chief in s4; changes need a new approval before publishing.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Discussion and explaining stay with people.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The police sergeant keeps community contact, custody decisions, issuing equipment and explaining procedures; compiling figures, phone rounds, books and rewriting procedures shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A sergeant whose admin is done by the end of the shift.

job.title: First-Line Supervisors of Police and Detectives
